title: Options in Bongbong-Leni VP row
primary_topics: Bongbong Marcos's election protest against VP Leni Robredo before the Supreme Court sitting as the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET)
PET Rule 65 'substantial recovery' threshold and Caguioa report on the three pilot provinces
Status of the Third Cause of Action seeking annulment of all votes in Maguindanao, Lanao del Sur, and Basilan
Four procedural options available to the PET and CJ's preferred path
sub_topics: Original protest covered 25 provinces and 5 cities, ~39,000 clustered precincts
Three pilot provinces: Camarines Sur, Iloilo, Negros Occidental
Recount result: Leni's original 263,473-vote lead grew by ~15,000 more votes
Romulo B. Macalintal as Leni's lead counsel; George Erwin Garcia as Bongbong's
PET Rule 65 quoted in full: dismissal authorized when protestant 'will most probably fail to make out his case'

people: Justice Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa (member-in-charge, pilot-province report author)
cases: Marcos v. Robredo (PET election protest, ongoing)

stances.claim: Leni's argument for outright dismissal under PET Rule 65 is doctrinally strong on the Second Cause of Action, because Caguioa's recount in the pilot provinces showed her lead increasing by ~15,000 votes -- fully satisfying the 'will most probably fail' threshold the Rule expressly contemplates.

However, dismissal cannot be ordered for the whole protest because Bongbong's Third Cause of Action -- seeking annulment of all votes in three Mindanao provinces (2,756 precincts) on grounds of terrorism, threats, intimidation, harassment, and pre-shading -- was not part of the pilot-province framework, so the Rule 65 disposal mechanism does not reach it.

Of four available options -- (1) outright dismissal, (2) adoption of the Comelec's 200-precinct TE, (3) full TE of all 2,756 precincts, (4) calling for position papers and amicus curiae briefs to craft proper rules -- Option 4 is the prudent path because the existing PET Rules do not cover the Third Cause framework, and no fair process can run without agreed-upon rules.
stances.rhetorical_move: four-way option enumeration with reasoned preference

stances.claim: Option 2 (using the Comelec's prior 200-precinct TE) would violate Leni's due-process rights because she was not a party to that other case and never had her 'day in court' on those findings.

notable_anecdotes: CJ's explicit disclosure that he 'vigorously supported' the PET resolution requiring both parties to comment, in interviews with GMA News and ANC's Karen Davila -- anchoring the column in his live public commentary rather than abstract analysis.

CJ's closing 'If I were still sitting in the Court, I would vote for the said option' -- a retired-jurist counterfactual that gives the column the weight of a draft dissent or concurrence without the constraints of an active role.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban dissects the four procedural options before the Supreme Court, sitting as the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET), in the Bongbong Marcos election protest against VP Leni Robredo. He sets out PET Rule 65's 'substantial recovery' standard -- which authorizes outright dismissal when the protestant 'will most probably fail to make out his case' -- and notes that Justice Caguioa's recount in the three pilot provinces (Camarines Sur, Iloilo, Negros Occidental) showed Leni's lead increasing by ~15,000 votes beyond her original 263,473. However, Bongbong's Third Cause of Action -- seeking annulment of all votes in 2,756 clustered precincts across Maguindanao, Lanao del Sur, and Basilan on grounds of terrorism, threats, intimidation, harassment, and pre-shading -- was not part of the pilot framework, so simple dismissal cannot reach the whole protest. Of four options -- outright dismissal, adoption of the Comelec's prior 200-precinct technical examination, a full TE of all 2,756 precincts, or calling for position papers and amicus curiae briefs to craft proper rules -- CJ rejects Option 2 as a due-process violation (Leni was not a party to the other case), notes Option 3 will take very long, and endorses Option 4 as 'the prudent way to proceed' since the existing PET Rules do not contemplate the Third Cause framework. He closes with the retired-jurist counterfactual: 'If I were still sitting in the Court, I would vote for the said option.'
